topics.title: 课程作业
topics.summary: 计分作业：如果教师规定不得借助外部帮助，使用生成式 AI 通常会被视为守则下的“未经授权辅助工具”；学校要求教师在课程大纲中写明规则。另外，即使课程禁止在作业中使用 AI，学生一般仍可把 AI 作为学习辅助（总结信息、检验理解），这类学习用途通常无需披露。
topics.scope: 计分作业的未授权辅助规则与学习辅助用途的区分。

claims.text: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

claims.text: The University of Toronto FAQ (updated October 2026) says undergraduate and graduate students may use generative AI tools as learning aids, for example to summarize information or test their understanding, in a manner similar to consulting books, peers or a tutor. Such uses are generally acceptable even if an instructor has said AI is not otherwise permitted in the course, and typically do not need to be cited or disclosed. If students use AI-generated information that would normally require citation (quoting, paraphrasing or reproducing text or ideas), they must cite it according to U of T Libraries guidance or the instructor's directions. Learning-aid use is distinct from using AI to complete marked work.

claims.text: The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

topics.title: 隐私与敏感数据
topics.summary: 在向任何 AI 工具分享个人信息或 2–4 级大学数据之前，须确认该工具已通过相应等级评估；AI Kitchen 工具获批至 3 级（模型比较工具仅至 2 级）。未经教师明确许可，学生不得把课程材料（课件、录像、试题、评分标准）上传到未获批的 AI 工具。教师使用未经审查的第三方 AI 工具时，必须允许学生退出并提供可行替代方案；收集个人信息时须做隐私影响评估（PIA）。
topics.scope: 数据等级、课程材料规则与第三方工具保障。

claims.text: University of Toronto Information Security guidelines state that no data should be provided to generative AI if any part of it should not appear in that system's results, and that before sharing personal information or university data classified as Level 2, 3 or 4 with any AI tool, users must verify the tool has been assessed by the university as suitable for that data type and level. AI Kitchen tools are approved for Level 3 data or below, except the Model Comparison Tool, which is approved only up to Level 2.

evidence.quote: No data should be provided to generative AI if any part of that data should not be included in results produced by that system.

A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

claims.text: Under the University of Toronto Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters (effective July 1, 2025), it is an offence for a student knowingly to use or possess an unauthorized aid or obtain unauthorized assistance in connection with any form of academic work. If an instructor has specified that no outside assistance is permitted on an assignment, the University would typically consider the student's use of generative AI to be use of an unauthorized aid. The Office of Academic Integrity scenario page gives the same example but still shows pre-2025 Code wording and is interpretive rather than the governing text.

claims.text: The 2025 Code of Behaviour on Academic Matters also makes it an offence knowingly to submit academic work containing a purported statement of fact or reference to a source that has been concocted (an offence depending on knowledge, including where the student ought reasonably to have known; not every AI error is automatically an offence). When an instructor has reasonable grounds to believe an offence was committed, they must inform the student immediately, give reasons and invite a discussion, normally held synchronously; nothing the student says in that discussion may be used in evidence at a hearing. The dean or chair must tell the student they may seek advice or be represented and are not obliged to make any statement. Sanctions available at divisional level include up to 12 months' suspension (up to 24 with Provost approval); suspension of up to five years or a recommendation of expulsion are for the University Tribunal.

claims.text: The University of Toronto does not support the use of AI-detection software on student work, because none has been found sufficiently reliable and sharing student work with such programs without permission raises privacy and ethical concerns. additionalTopics.summary: 在向任何 AI 工具提供个人信息或 2–4 级大学数据之前，必须核实该工具已通过学校相应数据分类等级的评估。中央 AI Kitchen 工具最高获批至 3 级（模型比较工具仅至 2 级）。教师在课程中使用未经审查的第三方 AI 工具时，必须允许学生退出并提供可行替代方案；涉及收集个人信息时必须进行隐私影响评估（PIA）。

claims.text: University of Toronto CTSI guidance on using non-supported (unvetted) AI tools in courses says students must be able to opt out: instructors cannot require students to accept a third party's terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property, and must provide a viable alternative where the tool is part of a required activity or assessment. A Privacy Impact Assessment is required wherever an unvetted tool collects personally identifying information, typically taking four to eight weeks.

evidence.quote: Students must be able to opt out. You cannot require students to accept a third party’s terms or hand over personal data or intellectual property. If the tool is part of a required activity or assessment, you must provide a viable alternative for students who decline.

This process typically takes four to eight weeks from the time all required information has been received.
